spans.t: This is a small book for ten days. It is made to go with the Camino Sanabrés, and it works just as well at home, one day at a time.
Every day has a morning reading of about five minutes and an evening reflection of about three.
In the morning
there are three parts.

items.t: The passage.
A few lines from
The Thoughts of Blaise Pascal
, quoted exactly as the translator, C. Kegan Paul, gave them in 1885. Pascal wrote in French in the seventeenth century, and the English keeps some of its age:
to-morrow
thou
whoso
. Read the passage twice, the second time aloud if you can.
The reflection.

This part is ours, not Pascal's. It starts from something you might meet on a road, an empty hour, a bench, a mist, and lets the passage open it. It says plainly what the passage says, where it is hard, and what it might ask of an ordinary day. It is allowed to doubt.
For the walk.
A question to carry for the next hour and one small practice that needs nothing but attention. You will not need a notebook.

spans.t: In the evening
there are two more.

items.t: At the end of the day.
A look back over the day you have just lived, with the morning's passage in mind. It asks two or three gentle questions and is honest about tiredness. The questions are for lying down with.
A short prayer.
Original and brief. If you pray, pray it. If you pray differently, change the words. If you do not pray, say it as a wish, to nobody in particular.

spans.t: Why this book for this road
The plan for this Library describes the Camino Sanabrés as a quiet inland road, and Pascal's
Thoughts
as the book of a restless mind meeting silence. A quiet road leaves a busy head alone with itself, and Pascal's notes keep coming back to exactly that meeting.

We have not walked the road, and we say nothing about it beyond what the app's own entry says: it begins at Granja de Moreruela and ends in Santiago de Compostela, and the app gives it no distance and no number of stages yet. Ten days is the length of this book, not a claim about the road. If your walk is longer, repeat a day or read on a rest day. If it is shorter, take the days that fit. The pairing is a recommendation, and Pascal's questions are the same on any road, or none.
A Christian book, and who it is for
The
Thoughts

are Christian. They are notes toward a defence of the Christian religion, written by a believer for readers who doubted, and in one meditation they speak in the voice of Christ himself. People walk the Camino for many reasons: faith, sport, grief, curiosity, a rest from work. All of them are welcome here. You do not need to believe what Pascal believed to recognise what he saw about restlessness, habit, doubt and silence. Where he is hard to follow, we say so, and we have left out the pages that would need a long explanation.
The shape of the ten days
The order is ours, not Pascal's. He left his notes unfinished, and editors have arranged them in different orders. These days follow a walk.

items.t: Days 1 to 3, the quiet.
A room with nothing in it, a reed that thinks, a sky that does not answer.
Days 4 to 6, what carries us.
Habit, the present moment, the reasons of the heart.
Days 7 to 10, what we are and what we risk.
Neither angel nor brute, the wager, the half-light, and a word of comfort.

spans.t: Day 8 is the wager, the argument of Pascal's that people know best and that is easily misread. We read it slowly and say where it is hard. If you are tired, read the passage and the prayer and leave the rest for the morning.
On the road and at home

Read the morning part on a bench, in a bunk, in a café while the soup arrives. Then put the phone away and take the question with you for an hour. You are very likely reading this on that phone, which is not the quietest room in the world, so the putting away is part of the exercise. Read the evening part last, when the boots are off.
Two words you will meet.
Albergue
is the simple hostel where pilgrims sleep, often in bunks, often with a shared kitchen.
Buen Camino
is what walkers say to one another on the road, roughly, may your Way go well.
Read slowly. Pascal's notes were written in pieces, on whatever paper was to hand, and they can be read in pieces too.

chapters.title: About the book and its author

spans.t: The man

Blaise Pascal was born at Clermont-Ferrand, in Auvergne, on 19 June 1623, and died on 9 August 1662, aged thirty-nine. His health was poor from childhood and never recovered. His mother died when he was eight, and his father, an official, taught him at home. The preface of our edition says that at fifteen his studies on conic sections were thought worthy of a hearing among the most scientific men of Paris. He was a mathematician from boyhood, and in later years of pain, the preface says, mathematics alone could calm him.

In the autumn of 1654 came what the same preface calls a second, sudden conversion. One night in November, from about half past ten until about half past midnight, he wrote a short record of what happened to him. It begins, after the date and the hours, with a single word:
Fire
. A servant found it after his death, sewn into a fold of his waistcoat. Before the year was out he had become, for a time, one of the solitaries of Port Royal, an abbey near Paris, and he wrote his
Provincial Letters
in defence of his friends there, in a long quarrel between two schools of the Church, the Jesuits and the Jansenists. The preface says the Letters put him at once among the great French writers.
The book

He went on to plan a work against atheists and unbelievers: a defence of the Christian religion, addressed to people who doubted it. He never finished it. What remains are the notes: a line, a paragraph or a page at a time, set down in his last years on scraps of paper and in the margins of earlier drafts, often when he was too ill for sustained work. Some were dictated to friends, and some to a servant. One of them says how he meant to go about it: "I shall here write my thoughts without order, yet not perhaps in undesigned confusion, that is true order, which will always denote my object by its very disorder."
The notes reached print in 1670, in a French edition called
Pensées

, which means thoughts. Its editors had edited them freely, and theologians had censored them. Later editors went back to the manuscripts, and because Pascal had not placed many of his fragments, each of them had to use judgement. That is why the order of the
Thoughts

differs between editions, and why our order is only ours. This translation follows the arrangement of the French editor Auguste Molinier (Paris, 1877 to 1879), in two parts: the misery of man without God, and the happiness of man with God.
Why it suits a pilgrim

It is a book of pieces, which suits a day of pieces: a few minutes on a bench, a rest at noon, an hour in a bunk. It is also a book about the very things a long quiet walk brings up. Why we cannot sit still. What we do with a silence. How a habit holds us up, and how a question holds on. One of the
Thoughts
is a single line: "Rivers are roads which move and carry us whither we wish to go."
Where it is hard

Pascal is not always an easy companion. He writes at length about prophecy, about the Jewish people, about miracles and about the quarrel between Jesuits and Jansenists. Those pages were written for readers of his own century and need more explaining than a day can hold, so they are not here. They are all in the book for anyone who wants them. The preface also describes his last years as years of austerity, self-denial and alms-giving, and a reader may feel that severity in places. Where a passage is hard, the reflection says so. The translation also uses words of its century, such as
heathen
and
Turks
, and writes
man
and
he
for everyone. We have left the words as they stand in the passages. They are the translation's, and they are not ours.
The translation, the edition and the licence

The English in the passages is by C. Kegan Paul, translated from Molinier's text. The title page reads London, Kegan Paul, Trench & Co., and the date MDCCCLXXXV, which is 1885. The translation is in the public domain. It is available from Project Gutenberg as ebook number 46921, and every quotation in this book was checked against that text, word for word. The file also holds a preface, notes and an index by the translator and editors. We quote none of that, only Pascal's own words.
What we changed in the passages is nothing. The old spellings stay:
to-morrow
sea-faring
starting-point

. Where we skip a stretch inside a passage, a mark like this shows it: …. The choice of the ten passages, their order, the reflections, the questions and the prayers are ours and they are original. Of the ten, six come from the first part, the misery, and four from the second.
Nothing of the Project Gutenberg licence text or trademark is copied here.
What happens in you when there is nothing to do?
The passage

paras.t: When I have set myself now and then to consider the various distractions of men, the toils and dangers to which they expose themselves in the court or the camp, whence arise so many quarrels and passions, such daring and often such evil exploits, etc., I have discovered that all the misfortunes of men arise from one thing only, that they are unable to stay quietly in their own chamber. A man who has enough to live on, if he knew how to dwell with pleasure in his own home, would not leave it for sea-faring or to besiege a city. An office in the army would not be bought so dearly but that it seems insupportable not to stir from the town, and people only seek conversation and amusing games because they cannot remain with pleasure in their own homes. … Hence it comes that men so love noise and movement, hence it comes that a prison is so horrible a punishment, hence it comes that the pleasure of solitude is a thing incomprehensible.

cite.t: , The Misery of Man without God, "Diversion" (tr. C. Kegan Paul, 1885)

spans.t: Reflection

Somewhere in the first days of a road there is an hour with nothing in it. The boots are off. The washing is hung up. The phone is down to its last few per cent, and supper is a while away. You are in a small room with a bed in it, and for once nothing needs doing.
Watch what your hand does next. For most of us it moves towards something: a screen, a map you have already read, a bag that does not really need repacking. It goes before you have decided anything.

Pascal spent a good part of his notes watching people do this. He looked at the courts and camps of his day, at the quarrels and the risky ventures, and decided that one thing lay under nearly all of it: people are "unable to stay quietly in their own chamber." A man with enough to live on, he says, would never leave home to go to sea or besiege a city, if he knew how to be at ease there. We do not really want the conversation or the games. We want not to be at home.

He even pictures the grandest case, a king with every comfort, and asks what the king's household is for. They are there, he says, to "think only how to divert the king, and to prevent his thinking of self." Take away the entertainments and the most powerful man in the country is a man alone with a problem he cannot solve.

The problem, in the same notes, is darker than the sentence above. At home you are left with yourself, and when we look at ourselves attentively we find "the natural evil of our weak and mortal condition, so miserable that nothing can console us when we think of it attentively." Noise is a way of not looking. That is why, he says, a day's hunting is not about the hare: people "seek the chase and not the quarry."

There is something worth saying here about quiet roads. Quiet is not only the absence of sound. A lane with no traffic and no talk may be the first place in months where your own thoughts are the loudest thing you can hear. That can be a relief or an assault, and it is often both before lunch.
Three things are hard in this passage.

The first is the size of the sentence. All the misfortunes of men from one cause? Hunger, fever and bad weather would like a word. Read it as "a great many of them" and it still stings, but it is probably an exaggeration, and you are allowed to say so.

The second is the man "who has enough to live on". Many people leave home because they must, and a quiet room is a comfort that not everyone has. For anyone grieving or lonely, it can be the loudest place there is. Pascal is not speaking to them, and nothing in the passage tells them to sit and bear it.

The third is that you have left your room, and by a long way. A pilgrim looks like the opposite of a man staying quietly at home. But Pascal's target is not travelling. It is flight, and the same walk can be either. You can flee yourself across a whole country, one village after another. Or you can use the road as the nearest thing there is to a quiet room with a view: a body that is busy, and a mind with nowhere to go but where it is. Which one your walk is, only you can tell, and the answer may change by the afternoon.

What does this ask of an ordinary day? Very little, and it is harder than it sounds. A few minutes without a diversion. Sit on the edge of the bed, or on a bench, with your hands empty. Three minutes is plenty. The point is not to feel anything in particular. It is a small experiment: see what you reach for, and see what comes up when you do not reach. Do not try to fix it. Pascal suspects that what comes up is the very thing the noise was for. You may find it is smaller than he thought, or larger, or only boredom, which has its own interest. It is also the one exercise in this book that needs no equipment at all.
For the walk

items.t: What do I reach for when nothing is happening?

For ten minutes of today's walk, go without music, podcast or screen. Choose the ten minutes now, before you set out, so that the choice is not made by a tired mind at the time. If your mind insists on running, let it, and only notice where it runs first. Then put that thought down and take the next step. Afterwards, notice how the ten minutes felt: long, short, or not like ten minutes at all.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The first evening of a road is often a quiet one, whether you meant it to be or not. The body has made its point. Whatever the day held is behind you now, and the room is small. If you can, put your feet up for this part.

If the quiet came to you today, even for five minutes, take it out and look at it. Was it empty, or only quiet? They are different things. An empty quiet feels like waiting for something to start. A quiet that is not empty feels more like a room that has been tidied: nothing needed, nothing missing. Some days you will get only the first, and that is simply the day's honest report.

Be fair to the hand that reached for the phone. It is not a vice at every hour. A message from someone you love, a map that stopped a wrong turn, a photograph of a door you liked: none of that is diversion in Pascal's sense. His word is for noise used to avoid something. Only you know which was which, and you do not have to decide tonight.

Try a rough count, without turning it into a score. Out of today's hours on foot, how many had something in your ears or in your hand? The answer may surprise you in either direction, and either answer says something about the day.

A word about tiredness. After a day on foot, quiet comes easily because the body insists on it, and it can pass for peace. It is a good thing, but it is not quite what Pascal was asking about, which is quiet when you are not worn out. Save that for a morning or a rest day. If tonight's quiet was only tiredness, that too is worth knowing.

If you are sharing a room tonight, the quiet will not be yours alone. There will be zips, breathing, the bunk that speaks whenever somebody turns over. You can still try a small version of Pascal's room: lie on your back for a minute and listen to everything in it, one sound after another, as if each were only one more thing the room contains. It is a way of staying in the room without asking it to be something else.

And if the quiet brought something up, a worry, a name, a loss, you do not have to deal with it in the dark at ten o'clock at night. Let it be noted and left until morning. If it is too heavy to carry alone, that is not a failure of the exercise. It is what friends and doctors are for. Tell someone you trust. In an emergency, 112 is the European number.

items.t: When today did I reach for something to fill a silence, and what was it?
Was there a minute that was quiet and not empty?
What am I carrying that I would rather not meet, and who could help me meet it?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for this room and for the day that led me to it. Let me sit here without hurry. If something hard comes, let me not run from it, and let me not be alone with it. Thank you for the people who made the bed. Let the quiet be kind tonight, and let sleep come easily.
Where does your worth come from, if not from how far you can walk?
The passage

paras.t: Not from space must I seek my dignity, but from the ruling of my thought. I should have no more if I possessed whole worlds. By space the Universe encompasses and swallows me as an atom, by thought I encompass it. Man is but a reed, weakest in nature, but a reed which thinks. It needs not that the whole Universe should arm to crush him. A vapour, a drop of water is enough to kill him. But were the Universe to crush him, man would still be more noble than that which has slain him, because he knows that he dies, and that the Universe has the better of him. The Universe knows nothing of this. All our dignity therefore consists in thought. By this must we raise ourselves, not by space or duration which we cannot fill. Then let us make it our study to think well, for this is the starting-point of morals.

cite.t: , The Misery of Man without God, "The Greatness and Littleness of Man" (tr. C. Kegan Paul, 1885)

spans.t: Reflection

By the second morning a number has moved in with you. Kilometres done, kilometres to go. It is a good number. It can be checked, it only grows, and it flatters. It also measures exactly one thing: how much ground your body has covered. The same is true of the stamps in a pilgrim's
credencial
, the passport that is stamped along the way. They are lovely, and they record where you have been. They do not record who was there.

That kind of measure is what Pascal means by space. Space is size, bulk, ground, the amount of the world you take up or cross. Set against all of it, he says, you are nothing much: "By space the Universe encompasses and swallows me as an atom." He grants that without a fight. Then comes the turn. "By thought I encompass it."

The picture he draws for this is a reed, "weakest in nature", but "a reed which thinks." The Universe, he says, does not even need to arm itself to crush a man: "A vapour, a drop of water is enough to kill him." On a hot afternoon that is plain fact, and a reason to carry more water than you think you need. But the reed has one thing the Universe has not. It knows. The Universe has the better of him, and he is aware of it, and "The Universe knows nothing of this." That awareness, small as it is, is where he puts our dignity.

It helps to be clear what he does not mean. He does not mean cleverness. The last line of the passage is not "think much" but "think well", and he calls that the starting-point of morals. As we read it, thinking well is closer to attention than to intelligence: deciding what to put your mind on, and doing it honestly. His phrase for this is "the ruling of my thought". You cannot rule what happens to you. You can rule, a little, where your mind goes. Every walker does it a dozen times a day without noticing: turning from the pain in a heel to the person walking ahead, from a grievance to the next bend, from a number to a hill.
Two things deserve a second look.

A dignity that rests on thought can sound like a good deal for the clever and a poor one for everyone else. Pascal knows the worry. A little later in the same section he writes "But what is this thought? how foolish it is!" and, a little further, "How great it is in essence, how vile in defects!" He is not boasting about the mind. What he points to is a kind of knowing that needs no cleverness: knowing that you are small, that you are fragile, that you will die. A very plain mind can know that. Even so, if the passage leaves you cold on behalf of people who cannot think straight, from illness or age or exhaustion, that is a fair reaction, and the passage itself does not answer it.

The other hard point is the bare line near the end. "The Universe knows nothing of this." The reed's nobility is lonely: a thing that knows it is dying, in a universe that does not notice. Pascal was a believer, and in other places he sets the reed inside a larger story. Here he leaves it standing in the open, and it is worth letting it stand there for a while before reaching for any comfort.

In practice, then, it asks you to stop letting the number tell you who you are. The day's worth is not its distance. A day on which you walked less far may have been the day you paid the best attention. A day when you covered a lot of ground may have been spent mostly in a mental argument with someone who is not there. Neither of those shows up on the count.

It also asks you to notice what bends. If the day is windy, find something in the verge that moves and watch how it takes the wind: it gives, and it stays rooted. Pascal chose the reed for its weakness. The part of us that thinks is not strong. It can be thrown by a hunger, a draught, a bad night. It is still the part that knows what is happening to the rest.
For the walk

items.t: If nobody ever asked how far I had walked, how would I measure today?

Choose one small question you care about, and follow it to its end on one stretch of road. Do not worry at it. Follow it, as you would follow a path, one step after another, and see where it comes out. When it has nowhere further to go, stop thinking and simply walk. If you find that you have been following it for a mile, that is allowed too.

spans.t: At the end of the day
You know tonight's number already. It was in your mind before you had your boots off. Try putting it to one side for a few minutes and asking what else the day held.

A day on foot is made mostly of small thoughts. To stop for water. To remember a name. To notice you had left something behind. To change your mind about a stranger. Pascal's "think well" can be as modest as that. Was there a thought today that you are glad you had? It need not have been deep. It might have been only the moment you saw that someone was struggling and slowed down.

There is a hard half to look at as well. Where did your mind run on its own, in circles, over something you could do nothing about? Not to scold it. A reed that thinks is also a reed that worries, and the worry is part of the same equipment. The point is only to see how much of the day it took.

Be honest about tiredness, too. The reed is bent tonight, and the Universe has not even had to try. The body is weak, and the mind at the end of a day is a poor judge and a worse planner. The kindest use of it is not to make it work harder. It is to stop it passing verdicts on you. Thinking well tonight might mean nothing more than not thinking badly of yourself.

If the mind will not stop once you are lying down, do not fight it. Give it something small and finite: three things for tomorrow morning, said once, and then put down. A reed in the dark thinks louder than a reed in daylight, and it does better with a short list than with an open field.

A good deal of what is done well in a day is seen by nobody. A bag moved from the path of someone's feet, a greeting returned, a decision not to say the sharper thing. Pascal's Universe knows nothing of the reed's dying, and it knows nothing of these either. Our reading, and it is only ours, is that this does not make them smaller. The knowing was yours, and it was enough while you were doing them.

Remember the others as well. Every walker on the road is the same kind of reed. The person who passed you this morning and the one you passed this afternoon are worth the same, and neither worth is a pace. Their number tells you almost nothing about them. If you caught yourself comparing, notice it, and let it go.
And since a drop of water is part of the passage: drink some before you sleep. It is a small act of thinking well.

items.t: Where today did I measure myself by distance, speed or someone else's pace?
What did I give my attention to, and was it worth giving?
What is one thought from today that I am glad to have had?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for a mind that can notice, and a body that carries it. Forgive me for counting the wrong things. Teach me to put my attention where it does some good. For tonight, let the day be enough, whatever the number was. Let the ones who walked slower and faster than I did be well.

chapters.title: Day 3. The silence of the spaces

spans.t: What do you do with a silence that does not answer?
The passage

paras.t: Whoso takes this survey of himself will be terrified at the thought that he is upheld in the material being, given him by nature, between these two abysses of the infinite and nothing, he will tremble at the sight of these marvels; and I think that as his curiosity changes into wonder, he will be more disposed to contemplate them in silence than to search into them with presumption. … When I consider the short duration of my life, swallowed up in the eternity before and after, the small space which I fill, or even can see, engulfed in the infinite immensity of spaces whereof I know nothing, and which know nothing of me, I am terrified, and wonder that I am here rather than there, for there is no reason why here rather than there, or now rather than then. … The eternal silence of these infinite spaces alarms me.

cite.t: , The Misery of Man without God, "Man's Disproportion" (tr. C. Kegan Paul, 1885)

spans.t: Reflection

On a clear night, away from street lamps, the sky is a different thing from the one you see on the way to a bus stop. There is more of it. The stars are thick enough to look like weather. If you stand still long enough, something happens that is not quite a thought: a sense of being very small and of there being a great deal of room.

Pascal went in for that feeling on purpose. In the pages just before this passage he takes the reader up first. The earth, he says, is a point beside the circle the sun describes, and that circle is itself a fine point beside the one the stars describe. He calls the whole of it "an infinite sphere, the centre of which is every where, the circumference no where." Then he turns the reader round and sends him the other way. Look at the smallest creature you know, a mite, and follow its body down through limbs, veins and drops. At the bottom, he promises, you will find a whole universe, with its own sky and its own mites, and so on without end.

"Whoso takes this survey of himself", the passage begins, and the self it means is what is left after both trips: a thing hung between two abysses, the infinitely great and the infinitely small, able to reach the end of neither. His word for the feeling is terror, and he is not exaggerating for effect, since he uses it again in the second stretch: "I am terrified".

What he proposes is not a cure. It is a posture. When curiosity turns into wonder, he says, a person will be "more disposed to contemplate them in silence than to search into them with presumption." This is the first of several silences in this book, and it is a chosen one. You stop trying to take the measure of the whole and let it be larger than you.

The famous line is the last one. "The eternal silence of these infinite spaces alarms me." It can be heard as a line about awe. Pascal wrote alarm. The sky does not speak. It goes on, in every direction, saying nothing to him, and he cannot take that calmly. Between those two silences, the one you choose and the one that is simply there, sits his question: "wonder that I am here rather than there." Straight after, he asks it in plainer words: "Who has set me here?" It is a question you may well ask in a bad hour, with a blister in mind, and it deserves its serious version too.

Just after the first stretch of the passage he gives the shape of the middle. What is man in nature? "A nothing in regard to the infinite, a whole in regard to nothing, a mean between nothing and the whole." A walker lives in that middle all day. The map of the whole country is one scale, and the stone under your boot is another. You are neither, and you move between them at the speed of a person.
Three cautions.

Do not feel obliged to feel what he felt. A sky can be frightening, or merely beautiful, or simply there, and none of these is a misreading. His alarm is his. You are free to feel awe, or nothing, or boredom.

Do not take "contemplate in silence rather than search" as a ban on asking questions. Pascal was a mathematician, and the pages around this passage are full of careful reasoning. What he is warning against is the person who sets out to understand "the origin of all that is" and is sure the whole thing can be grasped. The warning is about presumption, not about curiosity.

And do not skip over "no reason why here rather than there." There is a vertigo in the idea that your place and time are accidents. Some readers will find that bleak, and some will find it a relief, and some will answer it differently from Pascal. He answers it with his faith. You may not.

In practice: a minute of wonder without a verdict. Look at something large, or something very small, and do not explain it. The day is full of such things, and most of them go by while we are working out what to have for supper.

This is the book's title seen from the other side. On the first day the quiet was a room you could leave. Here it is the sky, and you cannot. The nearest you can come to peace with it, on his account, is to stop arguing with its size.
For the walk

items.t: What would I like an answer to, and can I get through one day without it?

At your next rest, find the smallest living thing within reach: an ant, a seed head, a beetle on a stone. Watch it for a minute. Then lift your eyes to the farthest thing you can see, a ridge or a cloud or a line of trees. Between the two, take two breaths in silence. You have nothing to say about either.

spans.t: At the end of the day

If the sky is clear tonight, and you are somewhere safe and close to a door, go outside for a minute. A garden, a terrace or a village street will do. Do not stand on an unlit road for the sake of a view. If it is cloudy, or you are too tired, nothing is lost. The same size is there above the cloud, whether or not you look. You can also take the trip with your eyes closed: the village from above, then the country, then the whole turning planet, and back down to your own bunk and the weight of the blanket. It takes less than a minute and it ends somewhere warm.

Smallness at the end of a long day is often a relief. The day's problems shrink to what they were. The argument you had with yourself at three o'clock, the weight of the pack, the thing you had to remember, all of them seem more modest under a lot of sky. If that happened to you today, it was a small kindness from a passage that was meant to alarm.

If it went the other way, and the size felt like a threat, that is his feeling too, and it is not an error. It passes, and it is usually worth a sentence to someone, a friend or the person in the next bunk, said plainly. Said aloud, such things often shrink.

There is a gentler version of his line about kingdoms: "How many kingdoms know nothing of us!" It applies to the road. You passed a great many houses today, and in each of them, from the inside, the day was the whole world. Someone was making soup. Someone was waiting for a phone call. None of them needed you, and none of them was a backdrop. They were the other half of the infinite, the half you can see.

The tiredness has a say, too. The body is a small thing, it has done a lot, and it wants a bed. Do not ask it for a metaphysics tonight. Questions about why we are here do not go away, and they will be as large in the morning.
The end of a day is also the hour of small bright rectangles. A minute of sky is a different use of the same eyes, and it asks nothing of them.

One more thought on the silence. It can be a refusal, or it can be a room. From outside, the two sound alike, and which one you are in may depend on who is listening and how the day has gone. It may even change while you stand there. You do not have to decide tonight which it is.

items.t: Where did I feel small today, and was it a fear or a relief?
What did I look at today without trying to explain it?
What would I like an answer to, and can I let it wait one more night?

spans.t: A short prayer

Whoever is listening, or no one: thank you for the size of the sky and the smallness of my day. Let me be quiet without being afraid. Let the questions wait until morning. Keep safe the people in the houses I passed, and the ones I have left at home. Let me sleep like something small that is not lost.
What are your feet teaching the rest of you?
The passage

paras.t: For we must not mistake ourselves, we have as much that is automatic in us as intellectual, and hence it comes that the instrument by which persuasion is brought about is not demonstration alone. How few things are demonstrated! Proofs can only convince the mind; custom makes our strongest proofs and those which we hold most firmly, it sways the automaton, which draws the unconscious intellect after it. Who has demonstrated that there will be a to-morrow, or that we shall die; yet what is more universally believed? It is then custom that convinces us of it, custom that makes so many men Christians, custom that makes them Turks, heathen, artisans, soldiers, etc. … We must acquire a more easy belief, that of custom, which without violence, without art, without argument, causes our assent and inclines all our powers to this belief, so that our soul naturally falls into it. It is not enough to believe only by force of conviction if the automaton is inclined to believe the contrary. Both parts of us then must be obliged to believe, the intellect by arguments which it is enough to have admitted once in our lives, the automaton by custom, and by not allowing it to incline in the contrary direction.

cite.t: , The Misery of Man without God, "The Weakness, Unrest, and Defects of Man" (tr. C. Kegan Paul, 1885)

spans.t: Reflection

By the fourth morning you no longer decide to get up. You get up. The boots go on, the socks go on first, and the pack is filled in the order it was filled yesterday. Nobody argued you into any of it. Your hands know where the torch is, in the dark, better than you do. A long walk is, among other things, a very long custom: the same movement repeated until the body no longer needs instructions. What that teaches the rest of you is partly up to you.

Pascal has a name for the part of us that does this: the automaton. He says that "we have as much that is automatic in us as intellectual", and he draws a conclusion that is easy to miss. A good argument reaches only the mind. "Proofs can only convince the mind." What we hold most firmly, he says, we hold by custom, which "sways the automaton, which draws the unconscious intellect after it." His example is a modest one. Nobody has demonstrated that there will be a tomorrow, and nobody doubts it, because it has come every day so far. Our confidence in the morning is a habit.

Then he applies the point to belief, and this is where he is most practical. Once the mind has seen where the truth lies, it needs the rest of the person to follow it. "Both parts of us then must be obliged to believe": the intellect by arguments, which it is enough to have admitted once, and the automaton by custom, over and over, by "not allowing it to incline in the contrary direction."

You can try this out on something much smaller than faith. You may be quite convinced that patience is worth having, and still snap at the person rustling a bag at six in the morning. The mind agreed. The automaton had not been told. Or you may be quite sure that you should drink water through a hot day, and forget until your head aches. What gets it done is not the conviction. It is the habit of a sip at every stop, repeated until it needs no one's agreement.
Some of this is awkward, and it is better to say where.

The list in the middle of the passage reads oddly now. It says that it is "custom that makes so many men Christians, custom that makes them Turks, heathen, artisans, soldiers". These are the translation's words, from its century, and the thought underneath them can unsettle anyone. If belief comes from upbringing, is it only upbringing? Pascal does not say so. He does not say that custom proves anything or disproves it. He says that custom carries what the mind has already seen, and that without it a belief wobbles.

Habit also cuts both ways, and the passage does not say so. Elsewhere in the same notes he writes, "There is nothing we cannot make natural, nothing natural we cannot lose." A habit of hurry is trained as surely as a habit of kindness. So is a habit of complaint, or of comparing yourself with the person ahead. The automaton learns what it is given. It does not ask whether it is good.

Then there is this: a habit can be a way of not being there. A walker can do a whole day on autopilot, feet and pack and snack all in order, and arrive having noticed nothing. That is Day 1's diversion in a different coat. The test is not whether you have habits. It is whether you can do them awake.

One more thing is worth saying before it comes up. This is the quieter cousin of Day 8, where Pascal makes the same move with more force and more risk, and invites a reader to begin with practices before the belief arrives. If you are comfortable with today's passage and not with that one, it is worth noticing why.

Which leaves the question of what to do with it. Choose one small repeated act and give it your whole attention each time. The road offers plenty: putting the pack on, taking it off, stepping over the threshold of the place where you will sleep, the first drink of water in the morning. Pick one, and let it be the place where you wake up. The mind decided once. Now let the body practise, slowly enough that you are there for it.
For the walk

items.t: Which of my habits did I never choose, and would I choose it now?

Pick one repeated moment today, such as putting the pack on, taking a drink or greeting someone, and do it the same careful way every time. Go slowly enough to be there for it. Do not try to feel anything. Let the repeating do the work. If you forget on the third or fourth time, begin again at the next chance, without commentary.

spans.t: At the end of the day

By evening, the habits are doing nearly all the work. Boots off, shoes on, wash, drink, find the charger. The tired body knows the sequence and runs it without asking you. That is what routines are for. They carry you when you cannot carry yourself, and it is worth a moment's gratitude to the part of you that learned them.

Now look at what else it carried today. Which habits served you? Perhaps a stretch before setting out, or a rest taken before you needed it, or a way of greeting people that makes the road friendlier. Which ones served you badly? A sharp remark that arrived before you chose it. A second look at the phone, and then a third. A grumble about the weather that had been practised for years before this road. The automaton does not discriminate. It takes whatever it has been given often enough.

You will have noticed something in how Pascal puts it, too: custom works "without violence, without art, without argument". It does not win by force. It works by being there every day, and by not fighting. That is a reason to suspect, though Pascal does not draw the moral himself, that small and steady changes may last longer than large resolutions made at night.

Pascal's picture has two halves, and tonight you might look for the gap between them. Is there something you have long been convinced of, that you should rest earlier, drink more, speak more gently, ring someone, that your habits have not yet caught up with? The mind has done its part. The gap is not a failure of belief. It is only that the automaton has not been taught.

Habits have bad days, too. A morning with a lost sock or a sore hip breaks the sequence and, with it, the calm it was giving you. The automaton is not a promise, and a routine that breaks is not a verdict on you. It rebuilds from the first act.

Which brings us to tiredness. Tonight is a poor night to reform anything. A tired mind makes bold promises and a rested one has to keep them. So do not resolve to become a different person. Choose a single act for tomorrow, small enough to do even on a bad morning, and leave it at that. The automaton learns by repetition, not by speeches. The last habit of the day sets up the first of tomorrow: water within reach, the pack half-filled, the phone put where it will not be the first thing you touch.
And if today went on autopilot from start to finish, and you cannot say what you saw, that is only information. It does not need a penance. Try tomorrow to be awake for one of its repeated moments.

items.t: What did my body do today without being asked, and was it good?
Which small act would I like to repeat until it comes without effort?
Where did habit stand in for attention today?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for the feet that know the way better than I do. Thank you for the habits that carried me when I could not carry myself. Forgive the ones that carried me badly. Give me one small act to make my own tomorrow, and the patience to repeat it. Let tomorrow's first act be a gentle one.
Where is your mind while your feet are on the road?
The passage

paras.t: We care nothing for the present. We anticipate the future as too slow in coming, as if we could make it move faster; or we call back the past, to stop its rapid flight. So imprudent are we that we wander through the times in which we have no part, unthinking of that which alone is ours; so frivolous are we that we dream of the days which are not, and pass by without reflection those which alone exist. For the present generally gives us pain; we conceal it from our sight because it afflicts us, and if it be pleasant we regret to see it vanish away. We endeavour to sustain the present by the future, and think of arranging things not in our power, for a time at which we have no certainty of arriving. If we examine our thoughts, we shall find them always occupied with the past or the future. We scarcely think of the present, and if we do so, it is only that we may borrow light from it to direct the future. The present is never our end; the past and the present are our means, the future alone is our end. Thus we never live, but hope to live, and while we always lay ourselves out to be happy, it is inevitable that we can never be so.

cite.t: , The Misery of Man without God, "The Weakness, Unrest, and Defects of Man" (tr. C. Kegan Paul, 1885)

spans.t: Reflection

Count, if you can, how many times your mind has been somewhere else since you set off. At the next café. At the bed you will have tonight. In the shower, which you are already enjoying in advance. In tomorrow's stage, in an email waiting at home, in a conversation from last week that you are winning this time. Your feet are on the road, and your head is mostly not. A day of walking is a long invitation to be elsewhere.

Pascal saw this in everyone, himself included: he writes "we" and not "they". We "anticipate the future as too slow in coming, as if we could make it move faster", and we "call back the past, to stop its rapid flight". Neither works, and we keep doing both. The result, he says, is that we wander "through the times in which we have no part, unthinking of that which alone is ours." The present is the only part of time that belongs to us, and it is the part we treat as a corridor.

He is not telling you to give up planning. The passage says plainly that we may "borrow light" from the present "to direct the future", and a walker who never looked ahead would be hungry and lost by evening. His complaint is about proportion. The present, he says, is treated as a means and never as an end: "the past and the present are our means, the future alone is our end." So we go through our days as a long approach to something else, and the something else never arrives as an arrival, because when it comes it is a present too, and we are already looking past it. "Thus we never live, but hope to live."

For a pilgrim this has an edge, because a pilgrimage is aimed at an end. It has a name on the map. There is nothing wrong with that. But the road to it is made of days, each of them as present as the last, and the person who walks the whole way thinking about the end has spent the whole way thinking about something that is not there.
A few things are hard here.

"The present generally gives us pain." That is not true of every morning, and it is not even what he says in the next breath: if the present is pleasant, "we regret to see it vanish away". Even the good moment is spoiled by watching it go. That may be a fair account of some temperaments and some days. It is a bleak thing to say about all of them, and he assumes that everyone is alike in this. You may already know which kind of walker you are, and you can decide how much of it fits you.

Pascal is not offering a technique, either. These days there are many schools of being present, and he belongs to none. He describes. As we read him, he thinks the restlessness runs deeper than a trick of attention can reach. That was the point of Day 1. So take today's practice as a small thing, and not as a cure.

And hope is not a vice. A person who did not hope to arrive, or to see someone, or to get better, would be in trouble. Read his last sentence as a warning about the balance and not as a ban. The clause about "a time at which we have no certainty of arriving" is blunt, too. You can take it as a fright, or as a quiet reason to enjoy the plain fact that you are, so far, here.

The practice is to come back, many times. Nobody can stay in the present for a whole morning, and the aim is not to. The aim is to notice that you have left and to return. It helps to have somewhere to return to: the sound of your steps, the weight of the pack on your shoulders, the temperature of the air on your face. One more word of ordinary prudence. On any stretch with traffic, the present is not optional. Keep your eyes and ears on it.
For the walk

items.t: Where is my mind right now: ahead, behind, or here?

Whenever you notice that you have left, and you will notice often, come back to your own steps. Count three of them. Use a bend in the path or a village sign as a reminder if that helps. That is the whole practice. Do not scold the mind for leaving. The coming back is the exercise, and every time you do it counts, however soon you leave again.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The day is over, and that is a rare relief. There is nothing left to anticipate until the morning except supper and sleep. For once the future is short enough that the mind can stop leaning into it. If there was a moment today when you were wholly where you were, take it out and look at it. It need not have been beautiful. It might have been a drink of water.

It need not even have been pleasant. A blister is the most present thing in the world. Pascal says the present "generally gives us pain", and a sore heel agrees with him. That does not make attention a pleasure. It only means that attention is real, and that a day is often more present than we give it credit for in the places where it hurt.

Take the pleasure you looked forward to most today, the shower, the chair, the cold drink. When it came, were you there for it, or already on to the next thing? It is a curious test, and the answer may well be "only partly". Anticipation can use up a good deal of what it hoped for.

Think about what you were always getting ahead of. For some of us it is rehearsal: speeches given in the head to people who are not there, plans for a stage that will arrive in its own time. The mind is trying to be useful, and a good deal of this is kindly meant. Still, count how many of the rehearsed conversations will ever happen, and how many of today's hours went on them. If you spent the day ahead of yourself, that is the common way to walk. It is not a failing. It is the very thing the passage describes, and noticing it is the whole exercise.

The past needs the same look. Did you call something back today, a remark you wish you had not made, an hour at home that went badly, a face? For tonight it is finished. You cannot change it by carrying it. You can only decide whether it goes to bed with you. Hand it over, in whatever way you like, to someone bigger than you, or just to the night.

Tiredness helps here, for once. A tired body makes the present compulsory: a heel, a shoulder, a hunger. You are present by default tonight, and it is fine to let that be restful. The one temptation at the end of a day is to plan tomorrow's stage in minute detail. Once is enough. The plan is made, and the plan can wait where it is until the morning.

If there is a meal tonight, try one small thing: take the first three mouthfuls with nothing else going on. No screen, no conversation, no planning. It is a modest way of being in the only place you have been all day.

items.t: When today was I wholly where I was, even for a minute?
What was I always getting ahead of?
What can I leave where it lies tonight, instead of carrying it into tomorrow?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for this day, exactly as long as it was. Forgive me for hurrying through the best parts of it. Hold the days I have left behind and the ones that are not yet mine. Let me rest in this one evening, which is the only one I have. Let the morning keep its own business.
What do you know that you cannot prove?
The passage

paras.t: The heart has its reasons, which reason knows not, as we feel in a thousand instances. I say that the heart loves the universal Being naturally, and itself naturally, according as it gives itself to each, and it hardens itself against one or the other at its own will. You have rejected one and kept the other, does reason cause your love? It is the heart which is conscious of God, not the reason. This then is faith; God sensible to the heart, not to the reason. Reason acts slowly and with so many views, on so many principles, which it ought always to keep before it, that it constantly slumbers and goes astray, from not having its principles at hand. The heart does not act thus, it acts in a moment, and is always ready to act. We must then place our faith in the heart, or it will be always vacillating. Men often mistake their imagination for their heart, and they believe they are converted as soon as they think of being converted.

cite.t: , The Happiness of Man with God, "Various Thoughts" (tr. C. Kegan Paul, 1885)

spans.t: Reflection

Sooner or later someone asks why you are walking. It is a plain question, kindly meant, put over a table or at a fork in the path. And a pilgrim's honest answer is seldom a list of reasons. What comes out sounds a little thin, or a little too large, or you hear yourself giving the reason that goes down best with the person asking.

Pascal would not be surprised. "The heart has its reasons, which reason knows not." The sentence is well known, and it is often taken to mean that feeling beats thinking. That is not quite what it says. For Pascal the heart is not the sentimental part. It is the part of us that takes things in at a glance, without steps: first principles, the sense that you are awake and not dreaming, the love of a person. Reason works slowly, with many views, and "constantly slumbers and goes astray". The heart "acts in a moment".

He is, remember, a mathematician. In another place he points out that nobody can prove by argument that they are awake: "We know that we do not dream, although it is impossible to prove it by reason". Reason itself rests on things it cannot prove, and he says it must "lean necessarily on this instinctive knowledge of the heart." He does not want either side to bully the other. It is "as useless and absurd for reason to demand from the heart proofs of first principles before it will admit them, as it would be for the heart to ask from reason a feeling of all the propositions demonstrated before accepting them."

The question in the middle of the passage is the one to carry. "You have rejected one and kept the other, does reason cause your love?" Think of someone you love. You did not arrive at them by argument, and a good argument against them would not stop you. That is not the same as blindness. It means love does not begin where reasons begin. Notice also the clause before it: the heart "hardens itself against one or the other at its own will." The heart is not only something that happens to us. By his account it can harden itself, "at its own will", and a hardened heart is something a person can work at undoing.

For him, faith belongs on the same side: "God sensible to the heart, not to the reason." That is his claim, and a reader does not have to share it to make use of the rest. The part about love and first principles stands without it.

The last line is the most useful, and it is easily skipped. "Men often mistake their imagination for their heart, and they believe they are converted as soon as they think of being converted." It is a brake on the first sentence. A strong feeling is not a conviction, and a fine thought about change is not change.
A few snags, then.

The first sentence is easily used as a licence: follow any feeling, it is the heart. Pascal's last line warns against exactly that, and he does not say how to tell the two apart in this passage. There is one clue. He says that we must place our faith in the heart "or it will be always vacillating." On that reading, the heart is the part that holds. A mood that comes and goes with the weather, with a good lunch or a bad night, is probably not what he means.

Then there is the sound of the first claim, that reason "slumbers". It can be heard as an attack on thinking. It is better heard as a description of a tool that works one step at a time and needs a place to stand. Pascal says it is the heart that supplies the place.

And there is the matter of what is left for readers who do not share his faith. A good deal. The passage about the heart's reasons does not require a creed to be true of friendship, of home, of the stubborn conviction that a person is worth trusting. Only the last move, the one about God, is specifically his.

For an ordinary day, that comes to this: be honest about where your reasons run out. When someone asks why you are walking, or when you ask yourself, give the first answer that comes. Do not improve it. Then listen to it, and notice whether it was an answer of reasons or an answer of love. Neither is wrong. But it is useful to know which one you gave.
For the walk

items.t: What am I sure of today that I could not prove to a stranger?

Notice one thing you like about the road: a light, a smell, the sound of your own steps on a certain surface. Do not ask why you like it. Let it be liked. If somebody asks why you are on this road, give the first answer that comes, unimproved, and hear how it sounds.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Look back for the moments that struck you without a reason. Not the postcard ones. Perhaps the way a door was opened for you. A smell from a kitchen. A stranger's laugh that made the whole hour lighter. Pascal records a friend, M. de Roannez, saying: "Reasons come afterwards, but at first a thing pleases or shocks me, without my knowing the reason". Often they do not come at all, and the thing was still real. Some of what struck you today was small enough to be gone by tomorrow, so it is worth a sentence now.

If you were asked today why you are walking, how did you answer? And did the answer change as the hours went by? It can. The first one, offered at breakfast, may not be the one you would give at six in the evening, and it is worth knowing which of them feels truer now.

Then look at the other side, carefully, because the last line of the passage applies tonight more than any other night. A long day of walking makes the mind prone to verdicts. Tonight you may be quite sure that this whole enterprise was a mistake. Or you may be sure that you have understood something very large. Both can come from a body that has walked a long way and eaten too little. Pascal's warning is that imagination can wear the heart's clothes. The cure for that is not to distrust everything. It is to leave the big conclusions until you are rested, and see whether they are still there.

Not everything the heart says deserves to be believed, either. Some of it is plain prejudice: the quick dislike of a face, the certainty that a certain person will be tiresome. Pascal does not exempt those. The heart's reasons need testing too, and the testing is reason's job. In his picture the two work together.

It is also a fair evening for letting reason have a turn. Is there something you felt strongly today that you would like to test by daylight? A decision, a resentment, a certainty about another person? Put it on a shelf for the morning. If it is the heart's, it will still be there, and it will probably be steadier.

And then the other direction. Call to mind, for a minute, someone you love without needing a reason, and let yourself simply be glad of them. If it is not too late to ring or message them, you might. It need not be about anything.

Be easy with the tiredness. A tired heart is still a heart, and a tired mind is still a mind. Neither of them has to be brilliant tonight. If all this is too much to hold, hold one thing: the person you thought of.

items.t: What moved me today without my being able to say why?
Where did I mistake a mood for a conviction?
Whom do I love without needing a reason, and when did I last tell them?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for the things I know without proof: the ground under me, the people I love, the pull of something I cannot name. Keep me from taking my moods for my heart. Let the ones I love be well tonight. Let me rest in what I know, and leave the rest until morning. Let me sleep without arguing.
Can you be gentle with yourself without letting yourself off?
The passage

paras.t: Man is neither angel nor brute, and the misfortune is that whoever would play the angel plays the brute. … Let man now estimate his value. Let him love himself, because he has a nature capable of good, but let him not therefore love the vileness which exists in that nature. Let him despise himself, because this capacity is void, but let him not therefore despise his natural capacity. Let him hate himself, let him love himself: he has in himself the power of knowing the truth and being happy, and yet has found no truth either permanent or satisfactory.

cite.t: , The Misery of Man without God, "The Greatness and Littleness of Man" (tr. C. Kegan Paul, 1885)

spans.t: Reflection

A long walk offers you two parts to play, and both of them are tempting. The first is the angel. The angel in you wants to be all will: a body that does what it is told, a mind that has no need of a bench, a stubborn refusal of every twinge. The second is the brute, which wants only to be comfortable, to be fed and let alone, and to call that wisdom.

Pascal says you are neither, and he adds a warning: "the misfortune is that whoever would play the angel plays the brute." He seems to mean something moral by it, an attempt to rise above one's own nature that ends up below it. The idea has a plainer version on a road, and it is only our reading, not his. A walker who goes on through a worsening pain to prove something may well arrive at the evening sour and short with everyone. The performance of the angel, kept up all day, turns into the manners of the brute by supper.

The second half of the passage is a piece of careful sorting. Pascal gives three orders that appear to contradict one another. Love yourself. Despise yourself. Hate yourself, love yourself. They stop contradicting one another when you see what each is aimed at.

Love yourself, he says, "because he has a nature capable of good", but not "the vileness which exists in that nature." That is: you are capable of more than you have done, and some of what you have done is not worth loving. Despise yourself, because "this capacity is void". As we read it, he means the capacity is still empty, not yet filled with anything, so that boasting would be silly. But "let him not therefore despise his natural capacity." The possibility is real, even though it has not been used. The passage ends on a restless note: a person has "the power of knowing the truth and being happy, and yet has found no truth either permanent or satisfactory."

A little earlier in the same section, he puts the whole thing as a picture of a king who has lost his crown. Our weaknesses, he says, "are the infirmities of a great lord, of a discrowned king." And near it: "A tree does not know that it is miserable." A tired pilgrim in a bunk does not feel royal. The point is that you feel your smallness as a loss, and a loss implies something that was once yours. The ache to be better is the evidence.

He is just as fair to the people who write about all this. A little later he says: "I blame equally those who take on themselves to praise man, those who take on themselves to blame him, and those who merely amuse themselves; I can approve those only who seek with tears." The flatterer, the scold and the cynic are all blamed alike. The only person he approves is the one who is looking for something and is troubled that it is not found. That is a useful standard for how to talk to yourself on a bad hill.
There are things to be careful with.

"Let him hate himself" is a dangerous sentence to hand to anyone. Pascal aims it at the vileness, not at the person, but some readers will hear a permission they have been giving themselves for years. The preface to our edition describes his last years as austere, full of self-denial, and a trace of that severity is in his pages. We do not recommend it. If you are already hard on yourself, take the first half of the passage, "Let him love himself", and leave the rest for another day.
The phrase about the capacity being "void" is not easy to understand, and the reading above is an interpretation. You can hold a different one.

And the passage is silent on a practical point. It does not say where the vileness is, or how much of it there is, or how you are meant to know. Self-examination without a stopping place can run on for ever. It is kinder to keep it short, and to do it in a plain tone.

Pascal does not mention feet. But if the angel and the brute are both mistakes about what a person is, the body is a good place to see it. A body is not an enemy to be beaten, and it is not an excuse to be indulged. It is the part of you that is doing the walking, and it has reasonable requests.

The order of things, then: body first, then self. At the next stop, do one kind thing for the body. Then do one honest thing for the rest of you. In that order. A blister seen to early is a small matter. A pain that is sharp, that grows, or that worries you deserves a doctor, and 112 is the European emergency number.
For the walk

items.t: Where am I playing the angel today, ignoring something my body needs, and where the brute, letting myself off from something I could do?

At your next stop, do one kind thing for the body: shoes off for a minute, water, a stretch. Then say to yourself, in one plain sentence, one thing you would like to do better today. Body first. Keep the sentence short, and do not add a verdict to it.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Look at your feet. It is the most honest inspection of the day. See what the road has done to them, and give them what they need: a wash, a dry sock, some air, a plaster where there is a rub. That is the passage, as we have read it, in practice. The body is neither to be despised nor worshipped. Thank the knees, the hips and the shoulders by name. A list of joints is a plainer litany than most.

Then go back through the day and ask where you played the angel. Was there a thirst you ignored, a rest you said you did not need, a pace you kept up because someone was watching? And what came after it? The pushing and the short temper are often the same hour, an hour apart. If the connection is there, it is useful to see it.

Ask also where you played the brute. This is not rest. Rest is wise. The brute is the shrug: the small thing you could have done for someone else and did not, because you were tired, and you were tired, and that was true. It is not a crime. It is only a place to look.

Try a different test, too. Imagine a friend telling you the story of today, with all of its shortcuts and all of its stubbornness. What would you say to them? It is often shorter, kinder and just as truthful as what we say to ourselves. You are allowed to use that voice on yourself, and it does not let you off anything.

Then, to balance it, there is the other half of the passage, which is easily forgotten. Pascal says: love yourself, because you have a nature capable of good. So name something good that you did today, and name it specifically. Not "I was all right." A particular act, however small. A sentence you did not say. A bag you carried. A pace you slowed for someone else.

The hour matters, too. Self-judgement is at its harshest and least accurate at the end of a long day. If the verdict you are giving yourself is a severe one, hold it over until morning. Judgements delivered at nine at night by a person who has been on the road since dawn are best treated as weather reports.
The angel forgets to eat. If you have not had enough to eat or drink since the afternoon, that comes before any reflection. The questions will keep.
If anything on your body is worrying you tonight, a pain, a swelling, something that does not feel like ordinary tiredness, that is for a doctor and not for a prayer. In an emergency, 112.

items.t: Where did I ignore my body today to prove something, and who paid for it?
Where did I let myself off when I could have done a little more?
What is one thing I did well today, named plainly and without a "but"?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for this body and its small mercies: feet that carried me, hands that held the cup, a bed. Teach me to be neither harsh nor careless with it, or with myself. Show me what is good in me, and what is not, without cruelty. Let me sleep like someone worth looking after, and wake up willing to do it again.

chapters.title: Day 8. The wager, read with care

spans.t: What would you risk, if you could not be sure?
The passage

paras.t: Let us then examine this point, and say "God is, or he is not." But to which side shall we incline? Reason can determine nothing about it. There is an infinite gulf fixed between us. A game is playing at the extremity of this infinite distance in which heads or tails may turn up. What will you wager? There is no reason for backing either one or the other, you cannot reasonably argue in favour of either. … Labour then to convince yourself, not by increase of the proofs of God, but by the diminution of your passions. You would fain arrive at faith, but know not the way; you would heal yourself of unbelief, and you ask remedies for it. Learn of those who have been bound as you are, but who now stake all that they possess; these are they who know the way you would follow, who are cured of a disease of which you would be cured. Follow the way by which they began, by making believe that they believed, taking the holy water, having masses said, etc. Thus you will naturally be brought to believe, and will lose your acuteness. … Now what evil will happen to you in taking this side? You will be trustworthy, honourable, humble, grateful, generous, friendly, sincere, and true.

cite.t: , The Happiness of Man with God, "Of the Need of Seeking Truth" (tr. C. Kegan Paul, 1885)

spans.t: Reflection
This is the best-known part of the
Thoughts
, and one of the easiest to get wrong, so we will go slowly.

Picture a fork in the path with no sign. You cannot work out which branch is right from where you stand. You also cannot stand there for ever, because standing there is itself a choice, and by dusk it will have made the decision for you. That picture is ours, not Pascal's, but it is close to his situation.

His question is the largest one: whether there is a God. The passage opens by granting that argument will not settle it. "Reason can determine nothing about it." Elsewhere he says outright that he does not mean to prove it by natural reasons: "Therefore I do not here undertake to prove by natural reasons either the existence of God". So the wager is not a proof. It is addressed to someone who has already concluded that reason is stuck and who would like to know what to do.

The part we have left out is the argument that gives the page its name. In it, Pascal's reader objects that the right thing is not to wager at all, and Pascal replies that this is not an option: "you are embarked in the affair." Not choosing is a way of choosing. Then he reasons like a man at a gaming table. What you stake is finite, he says, and what you stand to win is endless: "if you gain, you gain all; if you lose, you lose nothing." On that count, he says, a sensible gambler backs the side that offers so much.

The reader concedes the arithmetic and then says what he cannot get past: "my hands are tied and my mouth is gagged: I am forced to wager and am not free, none can release me, but I am so made that I cannot believe." That is where today's passage resumes. Pascal does not tell him to look for more proofs. He tells him to labour at something else, "not by increase of the proofs of God, but by the diminution of your passions." He points to people who were once where the reader is and who have taken up a way of life. The way includes practices, and the reader is told to behave as they do before he believes as they do. The reader replies with a fear, "But that is just what I fear", and Pascal answers with a question: "what have you to lose?"

In the stretch we have left out, between the second and third parts of the passage, he adds that his words are those of someone who has "thrown himself on his knees" to pray that the reader would also give his whole self. So it is not a trick played from a safe seat. Then comes the last claim: that the life this leads to is one of a person who is "trustworthy, honourable, humble, grateful, generous, friendly, sincere, and true."
It is hard in several places.

The register is the first. A gaming table, for the deepest question there is. To some readers it is cold, and to others it turns faith into an investment. Pascal seems to know how it sounds, since his objector is so uncomfortable with it.

The second is that the argument sees two sides: "God is, or he is not." Readers who see more than two live possibilities, more than one religion, or a God who would not be moved by a calculated bet, will find the odds less clear than Pascal does. The passage does not take that up.

The third is the advice: "making believe that they believed, taking the holy water, having masses said". These are Catholic practices, and to many readers they will sound like pretending. Day 4 is the background. For Pascal, custom trains the automaton, and the likeliest reading is that he is not asking for a lie. But it is fair to say that this line is hard to hear. And the objector's fear, of losing his "acuteness", is brushed aside with a question. Some readers will feel that the fear is worth more than that.

What is being asked of you? Not belief on command. If you have a faith, it asks you to be honest about whether it is held by the heart or only by habit. If you have none, it asks only that you not treat the question as settled before you have looked at it. And for a reader who finds the whole thing unconvincing, closing the book at this page is allowed. This may be the day of the ten most likely to irritate, and being irritated by it is a respectable way to spend a day.
For the walk

items.t: Which question do I treat as settled that I have never really looked at?

At your next rest, hold one question open for a minute without answering it: "Is there more here than I can see?" Walk a hundred steps with it and let it stay unanswered. If it irritates you, that is information too. If you catch yourself hurrying to answer it, slow down. The point is the minute, not the answer.

spans.t: At the end of the day
This is, for a good many people, the hardest day of the ten. If you spent it irritated with Pascal, that is a reasonable use of a day, and you do not have to apologise to a man who died in 1662.

Look first at something smaller. What did you risk today on something you could not be sure of? Setting out in uncertain weather. Trusting a stranger's directions. Taking a path whose end you could not see. A long walk is made of small wagers, and nobody had proved that the bed would be there. Pascal makes the same point close by, in his own way: "how much we do on an uncertainty, as sea voyages, battles!" Most of life is acted on without proof.

Then there is the sentence the objector says: "I am so made that I cannot believe." It is an honest place to stand, and Pascal's reply does not call it a sin. Whether you can believe, or cannot, or are somewhere in between, say it plainly to yourself, with no pretending in either direction. That is the one thing the passage cannot do for you.

His question can be asked both ways. "What have you to lose?" What would you lose by looking honestly at the largest questions? And what would you lose by never looking? You do not have to answer tonight. But both are questions with real answers, and they are different answers for different people.

There is a quieter use of the passage that needs no belief at all. Its last line is a list: trustworthy, honourable, humble, grateful, generous, friendly, sincere, true. Pascal says that whoever takes the road he describes will gain in this life, at each step. Leave aside whether that is so. Run your eye down the list, and ask which of those words today earned. Not all eight. Perhaps one, in an hour you had forgotten. That is a fair thing to take to bed.

One more thing, about people. Fellow walkers answer this question every way there is: some with a settled faith, some with none, a great many in between, and quite a few who have never been asked. The man who wrote this page, by his own account, prayed for the reader on his knees. You might ask yourself how you would treat someone who answered differently from you, and how you did treat the people you met today.

Tonight is not the night to settle anything this size, and nothing here needs deciding by morning. Tiredness makes big questions bigger. If you can, let this one be a question tonight, and sleep on it in the old sense: let it be there in the morning, unsolved but not lost.

items.t: What did I risk today on something I could not be sure of?
What would I honestly lose by looking at the largest question, and what by never looking?
Where is the line between taking up a practice and pretending, and which side of it was I on today?

spans.t: A short prayer

I do not know tonight what I believe, and I will not pretend to. Thank you for the freedom to ask. Let me be honest in either direction, and kind to those who answer differently. Stay with me while I do not know.
Can you walk by half-light?
The passage

paras.t: It had not then been just that he should appear in a manner plainly divine, and wholly capable of convincing all men, but neither had it been just that he should come in so hidden a manner as not to be recognised of those who sincerely sought him. He has willed to reveal himself wholly to these, and thus willing to appear openly to those who seek him with their whole heart, and to hide himself from those who fly him with all their heart, he has so tempered the knowledge of himself as to give signs of himself visible to those who seek him, and obscure to those who seek him not. There is enough light for those who wish earnestly to see, and enough obscurity for those of a contrary mind. … I may well love total darkness, but if God keep me in a state of semi-obscurity, this partial darkness is unpleasant to me, and because I do not see in it the advantages of total darkness it pleases me not.

cite.t: , The Happiness of Man with God, "Proofs of the Christian Religion" (tr. C. Kegan Paul, 1885)

spans.t: Reflection

There is an hour before sunrise when you can see your feet and not the horizon. The road is a pale line a few strides long, and the rest of the world is grey. Nobody waits for full daylight. You walk by what you can see, and the next stretch shows itself as you reach it. The same is true of mist, which turns a landscape into a room, with a wall that moves back as you move forward.

Pascal wrote about a larger half-light. The "he" of this passage is God, and Pascal is explaining a puzzle that troubled him as it troubles many people: why is the evidence for God not plain? His answer is that it is meant to be neither. It would not have been just for God to appear "in a manner plainly divine, and wholly capable of convincing all men", and it would not have been just either to come "in so hidden a manner as not to be recognised of those who sincerely sought him." So the signs are tempered: visible to those who look, obscure to those who do not. Hence the sentence at the heart of the passage: "There is enough light for those who wish earnestly to see, and enough obscurity for those of a contrary mind."

Read apart from his theology, it is an observation a reader may well recognise from other parts of life. The matters that count most, whether you can trust a person, what you want to do with your life, whether anything holds, are not settled by a proof that nobody can refuse. They show themselves in the measure that you look. There is usually enough to go on, and there is usually enough doubt for anyone who wants it.

The second stretch is the part that makes Pascal likeable. He admits that he does not enjoy it. He says he might even be content with total darkness, and that the in-between, the "partial darkness", is "unpleasant to me". In another note he puts the same feeling more sharply: "seeing too much to deny, and too little to affirm, my state is pitiful". It is a good sentence to carry for a day when you are neither sure nor sure of the opposite.
Here is where it is hard.

"Enough obscurity for those of a contrary mind." Taken by itself, that sentence puts the blame for doubt on the doubter, as though the dark were only for those who wanted it. Many honest people have been in the dark without wanting it, and some have wanted the light more than anything else. Pascal knows that.
