In the opening of the book he writes, "I can have nothing but compassion for all who sincerely lament their doubt." And as we saw on Day 7, the only people he approves are those who "seek with tears". The earnest, in his sense, includes the ones who ache at not seeing. The sentence is best read beside those.

The picture itself is also hard: a God who arranges partial darkness so that some will stumble. It is Pascal's claim, offered in a Christian book, and it is difficult even for many Christians. You are not required to take it as yours.
And the passage cannot tell you how to see better. It says only that looking is rewarded. That may be unsatisfying, and it may also be the only honest thing to say.

On an ordinary day it comes to this: walk the stretch you can see, without demanding the whole map. You do this constantly. You set out expecting the day to be the same sort of day as yesterday, and you trust people you have never met to have told you the truth about a path. Most of living is done by half-light, and it works well enough. The practice is only to notice that, and to let the half-light be what it is without treating it as a failure.
A safety word. This is for the mind and not for the route. If you do not know which way to go at a junction, stop and check a map, or ask someone. That is the right use of the light you have.
For the walk

items.t: What do I need to see that I cannot see yet, and what can I see well enough to take the next step?

At the next stretch where you cannot see the end of the path, a bend, the brow of a hill, a track going into trees, walk to the point where it opens, and notice that you could. Take the step without waiting to be certain of the one after it. If you are truly unsure of the way, stop and check. This is a practice for the mind, and not a licence to ignore a junction.

spans.t: At the end of the day
The evening has its own half-light. There is a quarter of an hour at dusk when you can still read the sky but the colours have gone. If you were out in it today, you had Pascal's lighting for free.

Think about what you had to go on without. The weather tomorrow. Whether the bed would be there. How the knee would hold. A stranger's directions, taken on trust. You acted on enough light, and the day went forward. It is worth saying that to yourself, because on a hard day it is easy to believe that nobody can walk without certainty, and the day is evidence that you can. A walker who waited for certainty about the weather, the bed and the knee would never leave the doorstep.

Then ask where you wanted more certainty than you needed. It is a strange habit. We check the forecast for a fifth time. We ask the same question of a person who has already answered it. We read the same page of the map after the route has become plain. Some of it is prudence, and a good deal of it is a nervous wish for the dark to be switched off. It is useful to know which was which.

There are two ways to end the half-light early, and both are tempting. One is a settled certainty, the other a settled cynicism. Each is a way of switching off the uncomfortable in-between, and each lets you stop looking. Pascal says plainly that he might love the total dark. Notice, without scolding yourself, where you reached for a simple yes or a simple no today, simply because the middle was tiring.

The hour is against you here. Doubt is heavier at night. The half-light seems darker than it is, and the largest questions come at the hour you are least equipped to carry them. If the dark feels heavy tonight, it may be partly the hour. The same question at six in the morning is often a smaller thing. Do not take a night's mood as a verdict on anything.

Last, think about who has been a light for you. A small one is enough: someone who pointed the way without being asked, a sign at the right bend, a message that arrived when you needed it. Light is often something that someone else has done. The same goes for how you saw the people you met. You saw a fraction of each of them, a face at a counter, a back on the path ahead. Everyone is in half-light to everyone else, and a little charity is the right response to knowing it. If you have not yet said thank you, there is still tomorrow.

items.t: What did I have to go on without today, and how did the step turn out?
Where did I demand more certainty than I needed?
Who or what was a small light for me today, and have I said thank you?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for enough light to take today's steps. Forgive me for wanting the whole map. Be patient with those who cannot see, and with those who say they can. Let me rest in the half-dark, and trust it for one night. Let me wake to the morning.
What if the searching is already part of the finding?
The passage

paras.t: Console thyself, thou wouldest not seek me hadst thou not found me. … Thou wouldest not seek me unless thou didst possess me. Therefore be not troubled. Be comforted; it is not from yourself that you must expect it; but on the contrary, expecting nothing from yourself, you must await it.

cite.t: , The Happiness of Man with God, "The Mystery of Jesus" (tr. C. Kegan Paul, 1885)

spans.t: Reflection

Whatever day of the road this is, it is the last day of this book, and a last day has a mood of its own. You may expect to feel finished. You may feel the restlessness of the first morning again, only more tired. The mind that came with you has been on the road all the time. It was never left at home, and it is, in its way, the main thing you have been walking with.

The three short pieces above come from a meditation Pascal called "The Mystery of Jesus", most of which dwells on the night in the garden before the crucifixion. Parts of it he writes as if Christ were speaking to the soul of the reader. The opening lines are in that voice: the "thou" is you, and the "me" is Christ. We say this plainly so that nobody mistakes the speaker. It is a voice taken from the Christian story, and Pascal means it to be heard as a word to someone who is looking.

What it says is quiet. Console yourself: you would not be seeking this unless you had in some way already been found. It is the reverse of the wager on Day 8. There he told a reader to stake everything. Here a voice tells him that his search is not a sign of an absence. The restlessness, which was the whole subject of this book, is turned round and read as a kind of evidence. The thirst is not nothing. Then the last sentence: "it is not from yourself that you must expect it", and so the thing to do is to await it.

Pascal gives his own reason, elsewhere in the notes, for reading restlessness in this way. We feel the lack of a happiness we cannot name, and he calls that lack "the mark and the empty trace" of a happiness that was once ours. A trace is always the trace of something. A footprint on a path is a poor sort of evidence, and it still means that somebody has walked there.

This closes a circle with the first day. There we asked whether you could sit in a quiet room, and Pascal said that most of us run from it. He did not think the answer was simply to stay in. In the same section as the thinking reed he sets two bits of advice side by side. The Stoics, he says, tell us "Retire within yourselves, there will you find your rest", and he says that is not true. Others say "Go out of yourselves, seek your happiness in diversion", and that is not true either, because sickness may come. His own answer: "Happiness is neither without us nor within us; it is in God, both without us and within us." Peace is not only in the room, and it is not only outside it. As Pascal means it, it lies with God, who is both outside us and within.

He wrote as one who knew something of this. One night in November 1654 he wrote a short record of two hours, which, his family believed, he moved from one garment to the next and wore until he died. In it, after the word
Fire

, comes the line "Security, security. Feeling, joy, peace." Further down: "Joy, joy, joy, tears of joy." He does not say how it came, and he does not offer it as a method. It is not a recipe for a Tuesday afternoon.
There are things to say about how hard this is.

These lines cannot prove anything, and they do not try. They assume what they claim: that you have been found. For a reader who feels nothing found, they are not a comfort. They are a statement that cannot be checked. They are best read as the consolation they are, a word for someone who is already looking, and not as an argument for someone who is not.

"Expecting nothing from yourself, you must await it" can sound like an instruction to sit still. It does not sit well with the rest of the book, in which Pascal says "Labour". The two fit together only if the labour is real and the result is not a wage. Do the work. Do not think you have earned the answer.
The meditation around these lines is a great deal sterner than these three, and we have left those parts out. They are all there for anyone who reads the whole.
And the peace Pascal wrote of did not make his life easy. The preface to our edition describes his last years as years of pain and self-denial. Peace and pain were in the same house.

What is asked is very small: to stop treating the searching as the problem. If you are still looking, for a faith, for a reason, for the next stretch of your life, then it is all right to be a person who is still looking. You can take that to a bench and sit with it. You do not have to arrive anywhere first. It also asks you to go easy on the other people who are still looking, and on the ones who have stopped. You will not always know which is which.
For the walk

items.t: What am I looking for that I may already have been given?

Stand still for one minute, on the road or on a bench, with nothing in your hands. Say, aloud or silently, in your own words: "It is all right to still be looking." Then go on. Let the minute be the whole practice, and do not try to make anything come of it.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Tonight is the end of the book, and it may or may not be the end of your road. The book cannot tell. If you are still walking tomorrow, take what follows as an interval. If you have finished, it is the last evening of something, and last evenings can be odd.

Look back along the ten days, not to summarise them but to see which stayed. The empty room. The reed in the wind. The sky that did not answer. The body that learned a routine. The mind that was always one step ahead. The heart and its reasons. The angel, the brute and the feet. The bet. The half-light. And this. One of them is probably clearer than the rest, and it may not be the one you would have guessed in advance. That is the one to take home.
Pascal's own book was never finished. The title page of our edition carries three Latin words,
Pendent opera interrupta

, which mean something like "the works hang unfinished". It is an odd thing to say on a title page, and an honest one. A book left unfinished is a fair companion for a walk that is not finished either, whatever the map says. You do not have to have finished anything.

If the road has ended for you today, the tiredness is a different kind. It is the tiredness of a thing being over. You might feel relief, or a flatness, or a small grief, or a good deal of nothing, and any of them is allowed. The feeling does not have to match the photographs. It will change over the next few days, as the body catches up with the fact that it can stop. Whatever you feel is allowed to be the whole of it.

It would also be good to spend a minute on the people. Think of three: one who made the road easier, one who made you laugh, and one you would like to ask about all this. You do not have to ring them tonight. It is enough to know who they are.

Do not judge whether the book worked. A good many things read on a road do their work later, in a kitchen, on an ordinary weekday, when the question comes up again. If nothing seems to have happened, nothing has gone wrong.

And think about the searching. Is there something you have been seeking, an answer, a faith, a way of being at home in yourself, that you have been counting as a failure because it has not turned up? Pascal's line suggests that the seeking may be part of the finding. You cannot know that tonight. But it might be allowed to stand, without a verdict.

items.t: What am I still looking for, and can I let the looking be enough for tonight?
Which of the ten days would I like to keep with me, and why that one?
Whom would I like to tell something about this road?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for the road, the quiet, and the company I did not always notice. I am still looking, and I am less afraid of that than I was. Whatever I have found, let it be enough for tonight. Whatever I have not, let me not be troubled. Let peace be a visitor I do not have to earn.

You have come to the end of the ten days, or you are stopping early, or you mean to go back to a day you skipped. All of these are fine. The book is not a course, and nobody is keeping marks. It was made to be a little company on a quiet road, and company does not have to stay once the road is done.
Ten small things
Ten small things fit in a pocket, and you have held each of them once already.

items.t: The room: a few minutes with nothing in your hands.
The reed: a worth that is not measured in distance.
The spaces: wonder before explanation, and a silence you can choose.
The automaton: one small act, done awake, and done again.
The present: coming back to your own steps, three at a time.
The heart: some things known without proof, and the care not to mistake a mood for them.
The angel and the brute: the body first, then the rest of you.
The wager: a question held open honestly, with no pretending in either direction.
The half-light: the next step by the light you have.
The consolation: the looking itself is allowed.

spans.t: Pick one, and let the others go for now. Choose the one you can remember without looking. It will do more for you than all ten kept in a drawer.
Going on

If you would like more of Pascal, he is easy to find. The edition we used, in C. Kegan Paul's translation of 1885, is on Project Gutenberg as ebook number 46921, and it is the same text every passage here was checked against. Our ten days come from the sections called Diversion, The Greatness and Littleness of Man (twice), Man's Disproportion, The Weakness, Unrest, and Defects of Man (twice), Various Thoughts, Of the Need of Seeking Truth, Proofs of the Christian Religion and The Mystery of Jesus. The Thoughts are short and can be read one at a time. The translator's preface and the notes at the back are not needed, and you can skip them.

A warning is fair. Much of the book is addressed to a reader who is being led, step by step, towards the Christian faith. We have left aside the long sections on prophecy, on the Jewish people, on miracles, and on the quarrel between Jesuits and Jansenists. They are his, and they will mean most to readers who share his world. If you read on, read what helps, and pass quietly over what does not.

Some of this will not have worked, and that is fair. A day that left you cold on the road may speak to you in a kitchen in March. A passage that asked for more belief than you had was not a test you failed. The wager in particular may have sat badly. If something barely touched you, put it down. Nothing has gone wrong.
A last word
At the start of this book we quoted a single line from the
Thoughts

: "Rivers are roads which move and carry us whither we wish to go." It is an odd little sentence to find among so many large ones, and it may be the kindest. A road that carries you is a road you do not have to push. Some of the best stretches of a long walk may be the ones that go on by themselves, while the mind catches up.

A mind that cannot sit still is not a fault peculiar to pilgrims. It is the common condition, and Pascal knew it better than most. What the road offers, if it offers anything, is a little room around that mind and a little time to see what it is looking for.
Walk again, when you can. Or tomorrow, to the end of your own street and back, with nothing in your hands and nowhere to be, and see what you reach for.
Buen Camino.
